names.name: Buffalo
names.said: Lower-cased on most menus now, which is what happens to a place name that becomes a flavour.

etymology.root: Buffalo, New York (the city) → attributive adjective meaning 'dressed in cayenne hot sauce and melted butter'; the city takes its name from Buffalo Creek, whose own name is disputed
etymology.first_attested: 25 August 1980, in the title of Calvin Trillin's New Yorker piece 'An Attempt to Compile a Short History of the Buffalo Chicken Wing' — the earliest dated printing this project can name, not a claim about the phrase's first use
etymology.note: The creek's name is argued over. The Buffalo History Museum records the Seneca reading 'Place of the Basswood' for the area, and separately the *folk* etymology that French speakers called it beau fleuve, beautiful river — that one first appeared in print on 23 March 1895, in an unsigned Buffalo Evening News review of a talk by Rev. Samuel T. Clarke, and the museum notes that no copy of Clarke's speech survives, so nobody knows whether he offered evidence. Second *folk* reading, heard at tables everywhere: that the wing has something to do with bison. It does not.

text.what: A city's name working as an adjective. Buffalo now modifies a sauce rather than a place: vinegar-based cayenne hot sauce cut with melted butter, and anything wearing it. The word travelled further than the bird it started on — it has been applied to boneless wings made from breast, to chicken fries, nuggets and popcorn chicken, to shrimp, to cauliflower, to dip and to pizza.
text.story:
Buffalo, New York is a port city at the head of the Niagara River, named for the creek. The wing took the city's name the way a garment district takes one: from outside. Nobody in Buffalo orders a Buffalo wing; they order wings, and the qualifier belongs to everyone else. *Inference —* that is the tell of a regional name that went national — the region drops it, the country picks it up.

The adjective then detached from the meat entirely. Once Buffalo meant a sauce, it could be put on a vegetable, and cauliflower dressed in cayenne and butter is Buffalo cauliflower without anybody claiming it is a wing. *Inference —* what carried is the flavour formula, not the animal, which is why the word survives a menu with no chicken on it at all.
text.how: As an adjective it takes the front of the name: Buffalo wings, Buffalo shrimp, Buffalo chicken dip. Where a menu wants distance from the city it writes 'buffalo-style' instead, and where a chain wants the heat named it writes 'medium' and 'hot' after it.
